full_judgment:
16. Every constitutionally trained mind will instantly click on and envision the Parliament at Westminster the moment it is said that the Parliament is supreme. The British Parliament has the plenary power to enact law. This power is uncontrolled, unfettered and unrestrained. No Court in Great Britain can refuse to enforce any Act of Parliament let alone declaring it ultra vires or unconstitutional. They, however, have the power to interpret the law and in so doing they have the power to remove elements unjust and unreasonable in the Statute upon the presumption of the Parliament's lack of intention of prescribing anything unreasonable and arbitrary. But ours is a written and rigid Constitution like those of the United States of America, India, Pakistan, Japan, Singapore, and others. Our Parliament is on and under a constitutional leash and circumspection. Here it is the Constitution and not the Parliament which is supreme. 

 38. None of the provisions of the PSA which I have very carefully scanned through does attract the mischief of Money Bill defined under Article 81(1) of the Constitution. Even then the Speaker issued a certificate saying that it was a Money Bill thus overstepping and transgressing Article 81(1) and 81(3) respectively of the Constitution. On that score alone the PSA is ultra vires the Constitution and therefore void. As regard the constitutional hurdle put up under Article 81(3) in Chapter II of Part V Legislative and Financial Procedure in respect of the conclusiveness of the certificate of the Speaker attached to an Act passed as a Money Bill is conclusive for all purposes and beyond question in any court and staunchly defended by the learned Attorney-General, Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with all the force at his command submits that the presumption of conclusiveness cannot be taken resort to as it does not attach to an unconstitutional act i.e the act of Certification by the Speaker in the instant case. 

 "The principle enunciated by the Indian Supreme Court that a law will not be held discriminatory when unguided discretion is given to a high and responsible officer on the expectation that the discretion will he exercised reasonably is difficult to accept. The expression 'reasonable' is vacuous unless used with reference to a specific standard and in the absence of a standard no exercise of discretion can be judged for reasonableness. Furthermore, in our society we have found high and responsible officers acting arbitrarily even though such arbitrariness is hard to prove in the absence of any standard of reasonableness, particularly in the face of presumption of legality of official acts. In Dr Nurul Islam's case the government urged the principle, but the Appellate Division rightly did not accept the principle even though the discretion was conferred on the government itself." 

 (3) the Criminal Process; a "fair trial" involves such elements as certainty of the criminal law, the presumption of innocence, reasonable rules relating to arrest, accusation and detention pending trial, the giving of notice, and provision for legal advice, public trial, right of appeal and absence of cruel or unusual punishment; 

 124. The argument of the learned Attorney-General that recording of the substance of the evidence instead of the testimony in its entirety as provided under section 18(1)(Kha) of the PSA does not in any way prejudice the accused in his defence because if the tribunal does not record the material evidence, it is a failure of duty of the tribunal for which the law cannot be bad and that if the tribunal omits something which is material, the accused can by filing a petition bring it to the notice of the tribunal and if the tribunal does not act on it, the matter can be agitated in the appellate Court, (the High Court Division) cannot but be said to be an ingenious and novel procedure because the accused is not required by law to prove anything in support of his innocence except when he sets up a plea of alibi. The burden of proof in a criminal case lies wholly and solely on the prosecution and it never shifts as it happens in civil cases. Because of the presumption of innocence the accused has nothing to say except that he pleads not guilty and claims to be tried. The prosecution must prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt. Inquisitorial system of criminal jurisprudence is an alien concept in the Anglo Saxon system which we have adopted. Thus section 18(1)(Kha) of the PSA is ultra vires the Constitution and void. The learned Attorney-General also defended section 14(3) of the PSA as to the use of a statement of a witness recorded under section 164 CrPC as evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act. This is also a novel concept alien to the law of evidence because such a statement can only be used by the defence to contradict the prosecution witness whereas under section 14(3) of the PSA the benefit is sought to be given to the prosecution instead of to the accused. This is against the rule of law as well as the due process of law and thus void. 

 The conclusiveness of the certificates of the Speaker attaches to an Act passed as the money bill when the Act is, in fact, a money bill under the Constitution. The presumption of conclusiveness does not attach to an unconstitutional Act for when any provision of any Constitution is violated Article 81(1) of the Constitution has clearly been contravened because the Act is not the money bill within that article. 

 Presumption as to the constitutionalism of law as passed by legislature. 

 210. When a law is challenged as unconstitutional there is a presumption in favour of its constitutionality. There is also a presumption that the legislature knows best the needs, requirements and aspirations of the people on whose suffrage it comes into being. When the court examines the constitutionality of legislation it does not claim that it is wiser than the legislature nor does it assume to exercise any right of veto on the power of legislature. 

 223. In series of decisions of the superior courts of this country held that if some of the provisions of the Act are invalid, those do not affect the validity of the whole Act as it remains. The cardinal principle of interpretation of the Constitution is that the constitutional validity of law made by the legislature is to be presumed valid unless the presumption is refuted. It is held by the Appellate Division in 41 DLR (AD) 30, SA Sabur vs Returning Officer Gopalganj: that the position of law on this point is that is must be presumed that the legislature is fully aware of the societies' problems and the legislature makes law to solve such problems keeping in view the welfare of the people. It also must be presumed that when any law is made it is constitutionally Valid until the presumption is rebutted by the person who challenges this validity. 

 250. There is always a presumption of constitutionality of a legislative qualification and the burden is upon him who attacked it to show that there has been a clear transgression of the constitutional principles. 

 251. It must be presumed that the legislature understands and correctly appreciates the need of its people, that its laws are directed to meet problems by acceptance and that its discriminations are made on that adequate ground. In order to sustain the presumption of constitutionality as to court may take into consideration of the matter to common knowledge, matters of common report, the history of the times and may assume over stay of facts which can be conceived, existing at the time of legislation. One who attacked a statute as being violative of the quality clause can do by burden of clearly establishing in vanishing of the statutes and a claim of violation of the quality clause cannot be upheld on mere speculation and conjecture.
